parts.text: But in spite of its historic popularity, the Mercator projection has long been recognised as problematic. The main issue is that, for

reasons, it artificially enlarges the regions nearest to the poles, making Africa – which straddles the equator – appear roughly the same size as Greenland, despite being about 14 times larger.

On September 4 2026, the UN passed a
tabled by representatives from Togo and backed by a number of African nations, to endorse and adopt a new world map. The map in question is the Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018 by prominent

Bojan Šavrič, Tom Patterson and Bernhard Jenny.

It will, in theory, replace the Mercator projection, which the Togolese campaigners say risks insinuating that Africa and its peoples are politically and culturally peripheral. The Equal Earth projection

this distortion by accurately depicting the relative areas of the continents.

This critique of Mercator is timely and important, and it also taps into a long history of disputes about how the continents should appear on the map.

from a different perspective.

I laugh when I see that, though many before this have drawn maps of the Earth, yet no one has set the matter forth in an
